notes.b: Your body takes energy in from food and drink and uses it up all day long. Comparing the two tells you whether your weight will stay steady, rise or fall.
points: Energy input is the energy in the food and drink consumed. Energy output (also called energy expenditure) is the energy the body uses for BMR (the energy needed just to keep the body alive at rest), physical activity, growth and digestion.
Energy balance is achieved when energy input equals energy output. Nothing is left over to store and nothing extra is needed from the body's stores, so body weight stays steady.
Positive energy balance means input exceeds output. The surplus is converted to fat and stored as adipose (fat) tissue, so weight is gained. Note that 'positive' here does not mean good.
Negative energy balance means output exceeds input. The body makes up the shortfall by using its stored glycogen first and then fat, so weight is lost.
Too little energy for a long time (underweight or prolonged negative balance) leads to weight loss, tiredness and poor resistance to infection.
Maintaining energy balance keeps a person at a healthy weight, helps prevent overweight and obesity and the diseases that go with them, and supplies energy for work, study, growth and activity.
notes.tip: If asked to define energy balance or outline its importance, say that input equals output and weight stays steady, that excess energy is stored as adipose (fat) tissue, and that a deficit gives weight loss. Remember positive balance is the surplus that causes weight gain.

notes.b: If a person is out of balance, there are only two levers: eat and drink less energy, or use more. Most advice combines both.
points: To reduce energy intake, cut back on sugary drinks, sweets, fried and fatty foods, and check portion sizes. Grilling or baking instead of frying, and avoiding snacking on high-energy foods, also lower intake.
Eating more fruit, vegetables and fibre helps because fibre fills you up, so you feel full on less energy.
To increase energy output, add daily walking, cycling, stairs instead of lifts, active leisure or a regular sport or gym, because each extra activity uses energy that would otherwise be stored.
To reduce time spent sedentary (sitting still), limit television, computer and gaming time and break up long periods of sitting.
A gradual change, sustained over time, is more effective than crash dieting, because it is a habit a person can keep up.
If weight problems continue, a person can return to balance with these changes plus support from a doctor, a dietitian or a weight management programme.
notes.tip: When recommending changes, tie each one to the cause you identified, and cover both diet and exercise.

notes.b: Case studies give a person's lifestyle and daily menu. The answer should analyse the energy balance first and then recommend changes, so work through it in order.
points: 1. Identify the person's energy output: occupation, activity level, time spent sitting, age and any growth or pregnancy needs, because these decide how much energy they use.
2. Estimate the energy input from the menu: note the high-energy items, such as fried foods, cakes, sugary drinks and large portions.
3. State whether the person is in positive or negative energy balance, and what this may do to body weight.
4. Recommend a change to intake: replace the high-energy items with fruit, vegetables, wholegrain foods or lean protein.
5. Recommend a change to output: name a specific activity, how often and for how long.
6. Write a one-day menu that meets the person's energy needs and matches the healthy eating guidelines: breakfast, lunch and dinner, each with two or three items.

Menus may be asked for a person who is obese, a teenager who plays sport, a person with a high energy requirement or a family with young children. A weight-reducing menu uses low-fat milk, grilled or poached foods, wholegrain cereals, vegetables and salad, fruit and water.
Diagram: none is needed. A simple balance diagram, with input on one side, output on the other and a tilt for positive or negative balance, is optional.
notes.tip: For an evaluate-the-menu question, identify the high-energy items, state the energy balance, then recommend changes to both diet and exercise. For a menu, give a reason linked to energy, with low-fat choices, fibre, fruit and vegetables, and water.

notes.b: Not all energy comes with goodness attached. Some foods give plenty of energy but almost nothing else the body needs.
points: Empty kilocalories (empty calories) are calories from foods that supply energy but little or no nutritional value, such as sweets, sugary soft drinks, crisps, alcohol, cakes and biscuits, and fried snack foods.

They add to energy intake without supplying protein, vitamins, minerals or fibre, so they can cause positive energy balance and weight gain while the diet is still poor in nutrients. Over-indulgence in sugary food can lead to obesity.
Replacing empty kilocalories with fruit, vegetables, wholegrain foods, lean protein or low-fat dairy gives the same or less energy with more nutrients.
notes.tip: Define empty kilocalories as calories with little nutritional value, give a sugary example, and say they lead to weight gain and obesity. Calories and kilocalories are the same thing.

notes.b: Obesity is a condition of excess body fat that harms health, usually caused by a long-term positive energy balance. Overweight is the milder stage. The causes below are mostly about lifestyle.
points: Energy imbalance: intake consistently exceeds output, so the surplus is stored as fat.
Sedentary lifestyle: a job or leisure time spent sitting lowers energy output, so more of the food eaten is left over to be stored.
Lack of exercise: regular physical activity is not part of the daily routine, so output stays low.
Psychological factors: depression, boredom and stress can lead to comfort eating, overeating and snacking.
Hormonal imbalance: an underactive thyroid gland slows metabolism and lowers BMR, so the same food intake produces weight gain. This applies to some people only, not as the usual cause.
Unhealthy eating patterns: frequent snacking, skipped meals followed by overeating, and frequent takeaways.
Poor food choices: a high intake of processed foods, sugary drinks and fatty foods. Large portion sizes of energy-dense foods also increase intake without adding to fullness.

In children, causes include sweets and fast food, sugary drinks, too much television and computer time, less outdoor play, advertising aimed at children, and parents using food as a reward. Genetic and family factors may also influence weight, but lifestyle causes are stressed.
notes.tip: Give at least two causes, each with a sentence of explanation of how it leads to weight gain. Obesity is not simply eating too much fat: it is any long-term excess of energy.

notes.b: Carrying excess fat for years strains almost every system in the body. Exams want each risk with a reason how it happens.
points: Type 2 diabetes: excess fat reduces the body's response to insulin, so blood glucose rises. It can be caused by a sedentary lifestyle and unhealthy diet.
Coronary heart disease and stroke: obesity raises blood pressure and blood cholesterol levels.
High blood pressure and high cholesterol, both linked to excess weight.
Gallstones: excess body fat increases the risk of gallstone formation.
Arthritis, joint pain and back pain: extra weight puts stress on the weight-bearing joints and the spine.
Breathing difficulties and sleep apnoea, and some cancers, are also linked to obesity. Varicose veins arise because excess weight increases pressure on the veins in the legs.
Depression and poor self-esteem, which can both result from obesity and make it harder to change habits. Difficulties in pregnancy and childbirth, and infertility, are further risks.
Reduced life expectancy, as the combined risks shorten life. Corrective measures are to return to energy balance and get support from a doctor, dietitian or weight management programme.
notes.tip: Give two to four risks, each with how it happens. The risks the marking schemes name are type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and heart disease, so lead with those. Add a corrective measure if asked.

notes.b: BMI is a simple measure that relates body weight to height and is used to classify body weight in adults. It is a screening measure, not a diagnosis.
points: BMI = weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared (kg/m²).
Below 18.5: underweight.
18.5 to 24.9: healthy weight range.
25 to 29.9: overweight.
30 and above: obese.
BMI does not distinguish between muscle and fat, so a muscular athlete may score as overweight.
Waist measurement is used alongside BMI, because fat stored around the abdomen carries greater health risk.
Children use age and sex charts, not the adult categories above.
notes.tip: Do not say a BMI over 25 always means unhealthy. BMI is a screening measure, so mention its limits when asked.

notes.h: Calculating and reading BMI from data
notes.b: Exams give you weight and height, or a table of results, and ask for a category. Follow the steps in order, and keep height in metres.
points: Step 1: convert height to metres (for example, 175 cm = 1.75 m).
Step 2: square the height (1.75 x 1.75 = 3.06).
Step 3: divide weight by the squared height (sample data: 70 kg / 3.06 = 22.9, in the healthy range). Dividing, not multiplying, is what gives the right answer.
Read a BMI table by finding the row for the height and the column for the weight, and matching the result to the categories above.
When comparing groups in data, note which group has the higher share in the overweight or obese categories and link this to diet and activity.
notes.tip: The common calculation mistakes are forgetting to put height in metres and squaring it, or multiplying instead of dividing. Show every step. In data questions, say which category each group falls in, compare the groups, and link to diet and lifestyle.

keyTerms.definition: The state in which energy taken in through food equals energy used by the body, so body weight stays steady.
Energy intake greater than energy output, with the surplus stored mainly as fat.
Energy output greater than energy intake, so stored fat and glycogen are used and weight falls.
A condition of excess body fat that carries health risks, usually caused by a long-term positive energy balance.
Body weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, used to classify body weight.
Calories from food that provide energy but little or no nutritional value.
Body fat tissue, which stores surplus energy from food.
A way of living with little physical activity, so that daily energy output is low.

factCards.definition: Energy output falls; the body needs less food energy, so surplus intake leads to weight gain; cardiovascular fitness declines.

questions.prompt: Give two causes of obesity and explain how each one leads to excess body weight.
questions.model: Energy imbalance: intake regularly exceeds output, and the surplus is stored as adipose fat, so weight rises. Sedentary lifestyle: low physical activity reduces energy output, so food energy that is not used is stored as fat. Also accepted: unhealthy eating patterns such as snacking, poor food choices with a high intake of processed foods, psychological factors such as boredom or stress eating, and an underactive thyroid lowering BMR.

questions.prompt: Discuss the health risks associated with obesity, and outline two changes an adult could make to restore energy balance.
questions.model: Health risks: type 2 diabetes, as excess fat reduces the response to insulin; coronary heart disease and stroke, as raised blood pressure and cholesterol damage blood vessels; high blood pressure; gallstones; arthritis and back pain from strain on weight-bearing joints and the spine; varicose veins; depression and poor self-esteem; difficulties in pregnancy and childbirth; reduced life expectancy. Changes: reduce energy input by cutting back on sugary drinks, sweets and fried foods, and by controlling portion sizes; increase energy output by adding regular brisk walking, cycling or a sport. Any change should be gradual and sustained, and the person's BMI and waist measurement can be used to track progress.
